### **Topics Taught by Siddharth**

Siddharth Saminathan provided instruction on caching, embeddings, and context window limits, emphasizing their importance in optimizing LLM system performance and cost.

#### **Caching**
*   **Core Concept:** Siddharth explained caching as a mechanism to store frequently accessed data for quicker retrieval, reducing the need to load applications or data from scratch. He provided a general analogy of previously opened computer applications being immediately accessible [2026-07-30, Page 1 — Siddharth Saminathan].
*   **Types of Caching:** He specifically mentioned "embedding cache," "LLM caching," and "prompt caching" as relevant types within the context of AI systems [2026-07-30, Page 1 — Siddharth Saminathan].
*   **Why Emphasized:** Caching is crucial for reducing embedding costs and improving efficiency by preventing redundant computations or retrievals when running operations repeatedly [2026-07-30, Page 1 — Siddharth Saminathan]. Himaya also noted that "it will reduce the embedding cost" [2026-07-30, Page 1 — Himaya Perumal].

#### **Embeddings**
*   **Core Concept:** While not explicitly detailing the technical process of embedding generation, Siddharth referenced "embedding generation" as a component of "System One" in the RAG architecture, alongside parsing, cleaning, semantic chunking, and vector store [2026-08-17, Page 4 — Siddharth Saminathan].
*   **Why Emphasized:** Embeddings are fundamental to the initial processing pipeline of a RAG system, converting data into a format suitable for retrieval and semantic understanding by LLMs.

#### **Context Window Limits & Token Economy**
*   **Core Concept:** Siddharth repeatedly stressed the importance of efficient "context engineering" and managing "token" usage within the LLM's context window. He explained that sending irrelevant information consumes valuable tokens and can lead to rate limiting [2026-08-07, Page 2-3 — Siddharth Saminathan].
*   **Inefficient Practices:** He highlighted the inefficiency of sending all retrieved chunks (e.g., 10 chunks) to the LLM when only a few are relevant, noting that if each chunk is large (e.g., 6000 tokens), 10 chunks quickly amount to 60,000 tokens, plus additional tokens for system prompts, leading to a total of 70,000 tokens for a single user turn [2026-07-22, Page 10-11 — Siddharth Saminathan].
*   **Optimization Strategies:**
    *   **Context Engineering:** Siddharth explicitly instructed trainees to "do some context engineering" to manage tokens effectively, rather than just relying on batching [2026-08-07, Page 2-3 — Siddharth Saminathan].
    *   **Re-ranking:** He guided Dakshinya to use re-ranking to send only the *relevant* chunks to the LLM instead of a fixed number (e.g., top 10) every time, thereby reducing token usage [2026-07-22, Page 11-12 — Siddharth Saminathan].
    *   **Efficient Context Window Utilization:** He advised trainees to make "the 1 million context window as efficient as possible," suggesting to "have 100, have like 30,000, 40,000 tokens of breathing room, front and back" [2026-08-07, Page 3 — Siddharth Saminathan]. This implies using the available token space strategically while avoiding unnecessary consumption.
*   **Why Emphasized:** Managing context window limits and token economy is critical for preventing rate limiting, reducing operational costs, and improving the efficiency and responsiveness of LLM applications [2026-08-07, Page 3 — Siddharth Saminathan; 2026-07-22, Page 10-11 — Siddharth Saminathan]. He noted that LLMs are not bottlenecked by finding relevant information within a large context, but sending excessive irrelevant data is inefficient and costly [2026-07-22, Page 11 — Siddharth Saminathan]. He also linked this to the challenge of dealing with thousands of rows and columns in an Excel file, where passing the entire JSON directly to the LLM would be "context heavy" and consume "very much" tokens [2026-07-14, Page 8 — Ganesh Krishna].
